Gag Me with a Spoon
GAG mee with uh SPOON
interjection, phrase (Gen X slang)
Valley Girl dialect of the San Fernando Valley, early 1980s; made famous nationwide by Moon Unit Zappa’s monologue on Frank Zappa’s single "Valley Girl" (1982), alongside barf me out and grody to the max. The image is of forcing oneself to retch with a spoon handle — a melodramatic way of saying "that is disgusting" about something merely uncool.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Gag me with a spoon was the Valley Girl’s verdict on anything beneath her: an outfit, a boy, a song, a lunch. It is disgust as fashion statement — nausea performed over trivia. The Christian observation is that disgust is a real moral faculty, given by God, and Scripture tells us exactly what it is for. "Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good" (Rom 12:9). "The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth" (Pro 8:13). God Himself has a gag reflex, and it is not triggered by bad fashion but by lukewarm religion: "because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth" (Rev 3:16). He says of hollow worship, "I hate, I despise your feast days" (Amo 5:21), and He lists the things that are an abomination to Him (Pro 6:16-19). The danger of the phrase is not its comedy; it is that it trains a child to feel revulsion at the uncool and indifference at sin. A father should let the joke be a joke and then retrain the reflex: be disgusted by what God abhors, and be slow to sneer at people He made.

Webster 1828 Definition

Valley Girl interjection (1982, Zappa’s "Valley Girl") for melodramatic disgust at something uncool; Scripture aims the faculty of disgust at evil (Rom 12:9) and shows God’s own revulsion at lukewarm religion (Rev 3:16).

GAG ME WITH A SPOON, interj. (Gen X / Valley Girl slang, early 1980s) That is disgusting; how gross; I can’t stand it. "He asked me to the dance? Gag me with a spoon!"

Companion phrases: barf me out, grody to the max, as if, totally.

Popularized by Moon Unit Zappa’s spoken part on "Valley Girl" (1982).

Webster 1828: GAG, v.t. 1. To stop the mouth by thrusting something into the throat, so as to hinder speaking. 2. To keck; to heave with nausea.

Decode for parents: the phrase performs disgust at the uncool; Scripture asks a child to feel it toward evil instead.

Key Scripture

Rom 12:9 — "Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good."

Pro 8:13 — "The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate."

Rev 3:16 — "So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth."

Amo 5:21 — "I hate, I despise your feast days, and I will not smell in your solemn assemblies."

Pro 6:16 — "These six things doth the LORD hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him:"

Modern Corruption

The phrase trains revulsion at the unfashionable and indifference toward sin; Scripture says abhor that which is evil, and shows that God’s own nausea is reserved for lukewarm hearts.

expand to see more

Misdirected disgust. Disgust is a God-given guardrail: the instinctive recoil that keeps us from rot. The Valley Girl aimed it at the wrong targets — at the uncool boy, the wrong shoes, the off-brand lunch — and a culture that recoils at the unfashionable while shrugging at fornication, cruelty, and blasphemy has its reflexes upside down. "Abhor that which is evil" (Rom 12:9) is a command to re-aim the faculty, not to lose it.

God’s gag reflex. The most sobering use of the image in Scripture is God’s own: the lukewarm church is spued out of His mouth (Rev 3:16). He is not sickened by the unpopular or the plain; He is sickened by religion that is neither cold nor hot. The phrase a teenager once used about a bad date is, in the mouth of the Lord, a warning to comfortable churches.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old Norse / Middle English gag (to choke) → early-1980s Valley Girl melodrama, popularized by Zappa (1982); Scripture re-aims disgust at evil (Rom 12:9) and lukewarmness (Rev 3:16).

1982 "Valley Girl" (Frank and Moon Unit Zappa) takes it nationwide

Siblings: barf me out, grody to the max

Biblical disgust: abhor evil (Rom 12:9); God spues out the lukewarm (Rev 3:16)

Usage

""Polyester? Gag me with a spoon!""

"Save the gag reflex for what God abhors (Rom 12:9), not for what the mall abhors."

"The Lord’s own nausea is at lukewarm religion (Rev 3:16)."
